issues.legal_issue: Certiorari is unavailable to quash an appellate tribunal’s in-jurisdiction decision on preliminary questions concerning an appeal.
material_facts: The petition sought certiorari against the appellate authority’s decision that the appeal could proceed, including its determinations about the appeal’s substance and the appellant’s standing.
The appellate authority was constituted to hear appeals in broad terms, without its jurisdiction being made dependent on a specified preliminary state of facts.
issues.conclusion: The High Court correctly refused certiorari because the appellate authority had jurisdiction to decide the preliminary questions raised before it, and an error made while exercising that jurisdiction would not make its decision a nullity.
issues.legal_principle: Certiorari does not lie merely because an inferior court or tribunal has reached a wrong decision within its jurisdiction; it is available where the authority acted without or in excess of jurisdiction, or violated natural justice. Where a legislature entrusts an appellate tribunal with broad appellate jurisdiction, that tribunal may determine preliminary matters such as appeal competence, standing, the order appealed from, and compliance with procedural requirements. The Court applied the distinction stated in Reg. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, 21 Q.B.D. 313.

predicates.certiorari_challenge: A party seeks certiorari to quash a decision made by an inferior court or tribunal.
predicates.appellate_body_has_general_appeal_jurisd: The appellate body is granted broad authority to hear appeals without jurisdiction depending on a specified preliminary state of facts.
predicates.challenged_questions_concern_appeal_prel: The challenged determinations concern matters such as appeal competence, standing, identification of the order appealed from, or appeal procedure.

issues.definition: When certiorari is sought against an appellate body’s determination of preliminary appeal matters within its broad jurisdiction, an error in that determination does not make certiorari available.

issues.legal_issue: A person permitted to contest an inquiry and whose contention is rejected is a person aggrieved entitled to appeal.
material_facts: The informant claimed an interest in the inquiry and in the property being declared evacuee property.
He filed a written reply to the property-holder’s statement and adduced evidence in support of his contention.
The authority rejected his contention that the property-holder was an evacuee and that the property was evacuee property.
The informant had also brought the matter to the authority’s attention and claimed a right to first consideration in allotment of the property.
issues.conclusion: The informant was a person aggrieved by the decision rejecting his contention and had standing to appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 24 of the Ordinance gives a right of appeal to a person aggrieved by an order under section 7. Rule 5(5) permits a person claiming an interest in the inquiry or property to file a statement and adduce evidence. A person allowed to contest a matter before the authority is aggrieved when the decision rejects that person’s contention. The Court relied on In re Lamb, Ex parte Board of Trade, [1894] 2 Q.B.D. 805, and Ex parte Official Receiver, 19 Q.B.D. 174.

predicates.statutory_appeal_from_administrative_inq: The proceeding is an appeal provided by law from an administrative inquiry.
predicates.person_was_permitted_to_contest_inquiry: The person was allowed to participate in the inquiry as someone claiming an interest in its subject or outcome.
predicates.person_submitted_written_case_and_eviden: The person filed a written response and presented evidence in the inquiry.
predicates.decision_rejected_persons_contention: The authority decided against the contention the person advanced in the inquiry.

issues.definition: A person who is allowed to present a written case and evidence in an administrative inquiry is aggrieved, and may appeal, when the authority rejects that person’s contention.

issues.legal_issue: A decision refusing to declare a person an evacuee and the property evacuee property is an appealable order under the provision allowing appeals from orders made in the inquiry.
material_facts: The authority conducted an inquiry into whether the person fell within the definition of an evacuee and whether his property was evacuee property.
After the informant contested the matter and presented evidence, the authority decided that the person was not an evacuee and refused to declare the property evacuee property.
issues.conclusion: The refusal was an order made in the inquiry and was appealable.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 7 and 24 of the Ordinance apply. Section 24 provides an appeal from orders made under section 7 without limiting appealability to orders granting the requested declaration. The authority’s decision whether or not a person is an evacuee is an adjudication under section 7; the power to grant relief includes the power to refuse it. The Court relied by analogy on Rayarappan Nayanar v. Madhavi Amma, [1949] F.C.R. 667.

predicates.statutory_appeal_from_administrative_inq: The proceeding is an appeal provided by law from an administrative inquiry.
predicates.authority_adjudicated_whether_person_met: The authority decided whether the person met the legal status test that determined whether the property received the claimed classification.
predicates.authority_refused_requested_declaration: The authority rejected a request to make the declaration sought in the inquiry.

issues.definition: A refusal is appealable when it is the authority’s adjudication of the requested status and classification in an inquiry from which the law permits appeals.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal’s incorrect description of the challenged order does not defeat it when its substance, grounds, and requested relief show that it challenges a different, related order.
material_facts: The appeal described itself as being against the later order concerning intending-evacuee status.
Its grounds and requested relief concerned the earlier decision refusing to find that the person was an evacuee and the property evacuee property.
The two decisions were made on consecutive days, and the later decision followed from the earlier one.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was, in substance, an appeal from the earlier refusal, and the error in describing the order did not defeat it.
issues.legal_principle: The appellate authority had jurisdiction to determine which order was challenged in substance. An error in describing an order does not prejudice a party’s right when the relief claimed and the grounds of appeal identify the order actually contested; the related decisions must be considered in context.

rule.if: statutory_appeal_from_administrative_decision and appeal_description_identifies_one_order and grounds_and_relief_target_related_order and orders_are_interlinked

predicates.statutory_appeal_from_administrative_dec: The proceeding is an appeal provided by law from an administrative decision.
predicates.appeal_description_identifies_one_order: The appeal’s formal description names a particular order as the one challenged.
predicates.grounds_and_relief_target_related_order: The appeal’s grounds and requested relief show that it contests a different order related to the one formally described.
predicates.orders_are_interlinked: The formally described order and the order targeted by the grounds and relief are connected, with one following from the other.

issues.definition: When an appeal’s substance targets a related order despite an inaccurate formal description, the appeal is read according to its grounds and relief, and the description error does not defeat it.

issues.legal_issue: An order written and signed before a party’s death is not invalid merely because it is pronounced after the death.
material_facts: The authority’s affidavit stated that the order had been dictated and signed before the affected person died.
The authority pronounced the order to counsel after the person’s death.
The challenge asserted that pronouncement after death made the order a nullity.
issues.conclusion: The post-death pronouncement did not invalidate the order.
issues.legal_principle: Applying the principle reflected in Order XXII, rule 6, of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Court accepted that an order written before a party’s death could be pronounced afterwards. The challenge was rejected in light of the affidavit that the order had already been dictated and signed.

predicates.challenge_claims_order_invalid_for_postd: The proceeding challenges an order as a nullity on the ground that it was pronounced after a party died.
predicates.order_was_written_and_signed_before_part: The order was written and signed before the affected party’s death.

issues.definition: An order written and signed before a party dies is not invalid solely because it is pronounced after that party’s death.
